PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Pre-menopausal breast cancer patients have higher tumor expression of the estrogen receptor gene ESR1 compared to post-menopausal patients.

Experiment objective: Evaluate the association between menopause status and tumor ESR1 expression.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
2. Normalize gene expression index by removing version suffixes.
3. Map ESR1 (HUGO symbol) to its Ensembl ID (e.g., ENSG00000091831) and confirm presence in the expression dataset.
4. From clinical data, select patients with menopause_status labeled 'Pre (<6 months since LMP …)' or 'Post (prior bilateral ovariectomy OR >12 mo since LMP …)' and drop missing values.
5. Intersect these patients with the expression matrix columns.
6. Extract ESR1 expression for each patient.
7. Compare ESR1 expression between pre- and post-menopausal groups using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
8. Create violin plots or box plots of ESR1 expression by menopause status and compute group summary statistics.

Deliverables:
• Number of pre- and post-menopausal patients analyzed.
• Descriptive statistics of ESR1 expression in each group.
• Test statistic and p-value from Wilcoxon test.
• Violin or box plot showing ESR1 expression by menopause status.

Analysis:
The experiment successfully loaded clinical and gene expression data, mapped ESR1 (ENSG00000091831), and compared expression between pre- and post-menopausal patients (n=224 and n=687, respectively). Descriptive statistics: pre-menopausal mean ESR1=4.11 (median=5.14, SD=2.72), post-menopausal mean ESR1=4.93 (median=6.27, SD=3.19). A two-sided Mann–Whitney U test yielded U=53719.5 (p=1.11×10⁻¹¹), indicating significantly higher ESR1 expression in post-menopausal patients. A box plot visualizing these distributions was generated.

Review:
Hypothesis: Pre-menopausal breast cancer patients have higher tumor ESR1 expression than post-menopausal patients.

Implementation: Clinical and gene expression data were loaded; Ensembl IDs normalized; ESR1 (ENSG00000091831) expression was extracted; patients with ‘‘Pre’’ or ‘‘Post’’ menopause status were selected (224 Pre, 687 Post); ESR1 expression distributions were compared using a two‐sided Mann–Whitney U test; and a box plot was generated.

Results:
• Sample sizes: Pre = 224, Post = 687
• Descriptive statistics (log2(FPKM + 0.001)):
  – Pre: mean = 4.113, median = 5.137, SD = 2.721
  – Post: mean = 4.932, median = 6.266, SD = 3.189
• Mann–Whitney U = 53719.5, p = 1.11×10⁻¹¹ (two‐sided)

Findings: Contrary to the original hypothesis, post-menopausal patients show significantly higher ESR1 expression than pre-menopausal patients (p < 0.001).

PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: African American breast cancer patients present with more advanced pathologic stage (Stage III/IV) at diagnosis compared to White patients.

Experiment objective: Determine if pathologic stage distribution differs between African American and White patients.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv.
2. Filter patients with race labeled 'BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN' or 'WHITE'; drop missing.
3. From pathologic_stage, classify stages into 'Early' (Stage I, IA, IB, IIA, IIB) vs 'Advanced' (Stage IIIA, IIIB, IIIC, IV) and drop ambiguous entries.
4. Build a 2×2 contingency table: Race (Black vs White) × Stage group (Early vs Advanced).
5. Perform chi-square test (or Fisher’s exact test if any cell count <5) to assess association.
6. Create a stacked bar plot of stage group proportions by race.

Deliverables:
• 2×2 contingency table of race vs stage group.
• Test statistic and p-value from chi-square or Fisher’s exact test.
• Stacked bar plot of early vs advanced stage proportions by race.

Analysis:
The code correctly loaded the clinical data, filtered for Black or African American and White patients, and classified pathologic stages into “Early” (Stage I–IIB) vs “Advanced” (Stage IIIA–IV). The 2×2 contingency table was:
  • Black or African American: 40 Advanced, 135 Early
  • White: 185 Advanced, 555 Early

A chi-square test (χ² = 0.2444, p = 0.621) indicated no significant association between race and stage group. The stacked bar plot confirms that both racial groups have similar proportions of early vs advanced stage at diagnosis.

Review:
Summary of Experiment:

Hypothesis: African American breast cancer patients present with more advanced pathologic stage (Stage III/IV) at diagnosis compared to White patients.

Data and Sample Sizes:
• Black or African American: 175 patients (40 Advanced, 135 Early)
• White: 740 patients (185 Advanced, 555 Early)

Contingency Table (Race vs Stage Group):
                  Advanced   Early
BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN    40      135
WHITE                       185      555

Statistical Test:
• Chi-square test of independence (all cells ≥ 5)
• χ² = 0.2444, p = 0.621 (two-sided)

Findings:
There is no significant association between race and pathologic stage group (Early vs Advanced) at diagnosis. The proportions of advanced‐stage disease are similar in African American (22.9%) and White (25.0%) patients (p > 0.05), so the hypothesis is not supported by these data.

Hypothesis: Burden of high-impact somatic mutations is associated with shorter time to new tumor event (recurrence) after initial treatment.

Experiment objective: Investigate whether patients with more HIGH-IMPACT mutations (nonsense, frameshift) experience earlier tumor recurrence.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_mutations.csv and cleaned_clinical_data.csv.
2. Filter mutation records for IMPACT == 'HIGH'. Count number of HIGH-IMPACT mutations per patient.
3. From clinical data, extract days_to_new_tumor and new_tumor_event (YES/NO); drop patients without recurrence information.
4. Merge high-impact mutation counts with recurrence data.
5. Compute Spearman correlation between high-impact count and days_to_new_tumor among patients with an event.
6. Dichotomize patients at the median high-impact count into High vs Low groups and compare time to recurrence via Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank test.
7. Optionally adjust for clinical covariates (age, stage) in a Cox model with high-impact count as predictor.
8. Visualize scatter plot of mutation count vs time to recurrence and KM curves.

Deliverables:
• Spearman correlation coefficient and p-value.
• Kaplan–Meier plot of recurrence-free survival by high-impact burden with log-rank p-value.
• Cox model summary if adjusted analysis is performed.
• Scatter plot with regression line showing mutation count vs days_to_new_tumor.

content:
{"code":"import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

# Survival analysis imports
try:
    from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter, CoxPHFitter
    from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test
except ImportError:
    import subprocess, sys
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, '-m', 'pip', 'install', '--quiet', 'lifelines'])
    from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter, CoxPHFitter
    from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test

# 1. Load data
clin = pd.read_csv('cleaned_clinical_data.csv')
mut = pd.read_csv('cleaned_mutations.csv')

# 2. Count HIGH impact mutations per patient
high_mut = mut[mut['IMPACT'] == 'HIGH']
hi_counts = high_mut.groupby('bcr_patient_barcode').size().rename('high_impact_count')

# 3. Prepare clinical recurrence data
clin2 = clin[['bcr_patient_barcode', 'new_tumor_event', 'days_to_new_tumor', 'days_to_last_followup', 'age_at_diagnosis']].copy()
# Drop patients without any follow-up time
clin2 = clin2.dropna(subset=['days_to_last_followup'])

# 4. Merge
df = clin2.set_index('bcr_patient_barcode').join(hi_counts).fillna({'high_impact_count': 0}).reset_index()
# Define survival times
# For event YES, use days_to_new_tumor; else censor at last_followup
df['duration'] = np.where(df['new_tumor_event'] == 'YES', df['days_to_new_tumor'], df['days_to_last_followup'])
# Drop missing durations
df = df.dropna(subset=['duration'])
# Event observed flag
df['event'] = (df['new_tumor_event'] == 'YES').astype(int)

print(f"Total patients with data: {len(df)}")

# 5. Spearman correlation among patients with event
evt = df[df['event'] == 1]
rho, pval = spearmanr(evt['high_impact_count'], evt['days_to_new_tumor'], nan_policy='omit')
print(f"Spearman correlation (HIGH-impact count vs days_to_new_tumor) among events: rho={rho:.3f}, p={pval:.3e}")

# Scatter plot
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.regplot(x='high_impact_count', y='days_to_new_tumor', data=evt, scatter_kws={'alpha':0.6})
plt.xlabel('High-impact mutation count')
plt.ylabel('Days to new tumor event')
plt.title('Mutation burden vs Time to Recurrence')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. Dichotomize at median
median_count = df['high_impact_count'].median()
df['group'] = np.where(df['high_impact_count'] > median_count, 'High', 'Low')
print(f"Median high-impact count = {median_count}. Group sizes: {df['group'].value_counts().to_dict()}")

# KM curves
kmf_high = KaplanMeierFitter()
kmf_low = KaplanMeierFitter()

high_df = df[df['group'] == 'High']
low_df = df[df['group'] == 'Low']

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
kmf_high.fit(high_df['duration'], high_df['event'], label='High burden')
kmf_low.fit(low_df['duration'], low_df['event'], label='Low burden')
kmf_high.plot(ci_show=False)
kmf_low.plot(ci_show=False)
plt.xlabel('Days')
plt.ylabel('Recurrence-free Survival Probability')
plt.title('KM Curves by Mutation Burden')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Log-rank test
results = logrank_test(high_df['duration'], low_df['duration'], high_df['event'], low_df['event'])
print(f"Log-rank test: chi2={results.test_statistic:.3f}, p={results.p_value:.3e}")

# 7. Cox proportional hazards model (adjusting for age)
cox_df = df[['duration', 'event', 'high_impact_count', 'age_at_diagnosis']].dropna()
cph = CoxPHFitter()
cph.fit(cox_df, duration_col='duration', event_col='event')
